examples.solution_text:
Multiply the number of cubes in one layer by the number of layers.

Prism A has $8\times3=24$ cubes in each layer and $2$ layers.
$\begin{aligned}24\times2&=48\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

Prism B has $4\times3=12$ cubes in each layer and $4$ layers.
$\begin{aligned}12\times4&=48\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

Both volumes are $48\text{ cm}^3$, although the dimensions are different.

examples.question_text: A student says, “Rectangular prisms with equal volumes must have the same height.” Compare a prism with length $3$ cm, width $4$ cm and height $5$ cm with one having length $5$ cm, width $6$ cm and height $2$ cm. Is the student correct?
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{aligned}3\times4\times5&=60\text{ cm}^3\\5\times6\times2&=60\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

The student is incorrect. The volumes are equal, but the heights are $5$ cm and $2$ cm.

Changing the order of the same three dimensions also preserves volume because multiplication can be done in any order.

examples.question_text: Give two rectangular prisms with different whole-number dimensions and volume $40\text{ cm}^3$. Changing only the order of the dimensions does not count as a different prism.
examples.solution_text:
Choose two dimensions, then divide the volume by their product to find the third.

For length $2$ cm and width $4$ cm:
$\begin{aligned}40\div(2\times4)&=40\div8\\&=5\end{aligned}$

For length $1$ cm and width $5$ cm:
$\begin{aligned}40\div(1\times5)&=40\div5\\&=8\end{aligned}$

Sample dimensions are $2$ cm by $4$ cm by $5$ cm and $1$ cm by $5$ cm by $8$ cm.

Check:
$\begin{aligned}2\times4\times5&=40\\1\times5\times8&=40\end{aligned}$

examples.question_text: List all whole-number dimension triples for rectangular prisms with volume $18\text{ cm}^3$. Count rearrangements of the same three dimensions only once.
examples.solution_text:
Write each triple from smallest to largest.

With smallest dimension $1$ cm, the other two dimensions must multiply to $18$:
$1\times1\times18$, $1\times2\times9$, $1\times3\times6$.

With smallest dimension $2$ cm, the other two dimensions must multiply to $9$:
$2\times3\times3$.

A smallest dimension of $3$ cm or more would give a volume of at least $3\times3\times3=27\text{ cm}^3$, so there are no more triples.

The four dimension triples, in centimetres, are $(1,1,18)$, $(1,2,9)$, $(1,3,6)$ and $(2,3,3)$.

examples.question_text: Prism A has length $3$ cm, width $4$ cm and height $7$ cm. Prism B has length $2$ cm and width $6$ cm. Find the height of prism B so that the volumes are equal.
examples.solution_text:
Find prism A's volume:
$\begin{aligned}3\times4\times7&=12\times7\\&=84\text{ cm}^3\end{aligned}$

Prism B has $2\times6=12$ cubes in one layer. Find the number of layers:
$\begin{aligned}84\div12&=7\end{aligned}$

Prism B's height is $7$ cm.

Check: $2\times6\times7=84\text{ cm}^3$.

examples.question_text: A rectangular prism of modelling material has length $4$ m, width $3$ m and height $5$ m. It is reshaped into a rectangular prism with length $5$ m and width $6$ m, keeping the same volume. Find its new height.
examples.solution_text:
Find the original volume:
$\begin{aligned}4\times3\times5&=12\times5\\&=60\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$

The new prism has $5\times6=30$ cubic-metre blocks in each $1$ m-high layer.
$\begin{aligned}60\div30&=2\end{aligned}$

The new height is $2$ m.

Check: $5\times6\times2=60\text{ m}^3$.

examples.derivation: Prism A: 8 × 3 = 24 cubes per layer; 24 × 2 = 48 cm³. Prism B: 4 × 3 = 12 cubes per layer; 12 × 4 = 48 cm³. Different dimensions give equal volumes. Diagram labels agree with these dimensions.
3 × 4 × 5 = 60 cm³ and 5 × 6 × 2 = 60 cm³. Heights 5 cm and 2 cm differ, disproving the claim. Reordering multiplication factors also preserves their product.
40 ÷ (2 × 4) = 5 and 40 ÷ (1 × 5) = 8. The triples (2,4,5) and (1,5,8) each multiply to 40 and are not rearrangements of each other.

For ordered positive dimensions a ≤ b ≤ c, a = 1 gives factor pairs (1,18), (2,9), and (3,6). For a = 2, bc = 9 gives (3,3). For a ≥ 3, abc ≥ 27 > 18. Thus exactly four unordered triples give 18 cm³: (1,1,18), (1,2,9), (1,3,6), and (2,3,3).
Prism A has volume 3 × 4 × 7 = 84 cm³. Prism B has 2 × 6 = 12 cubes per layer, so 84 ÷ 12 = 7 layers and height 7 cm. Check: 2 × 6 × 7 = 84 cm³.
Original volume: 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 m³. Each new 1 m-high layer contains 5 × 6 = 30 cubic-metre blocks. Therefore 60 ÷ 30 = 2 layers and new height 2 m. Check: 5 × 6 × 2 = 60 m³.
